query: For transition-metal catalysts, formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify it.

decision.trend: Early work on Pt-based and Pt-alloy catalysts showed that electronic structure and local atomic arrangement affect catalytic turnover sites (PMC4931244). Single-atom alloy approaches then highlighted how tailored adsorption energies could break scaling relations to enhance selectivity and conversion simultaneously (PMC6203812). More recent insights into multicomponent high-entropy metal compositions revealed that heterogeneity of local electronic environments can reshape intermediate adsorption and break conventional Sabatier limitations (PMC9106752, PMC10774414). Despite these advances, the precise mechanistic picture—how local electronic structures and dynamic surface configurations jointly govern activity, selectivity, and durability—remains incompletely understood.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear which specific local electronic/structural features overwhelmingly dictate catalytic performance under reaction conditions and how these evolve during continuous operation. A fully validated mechanistic framework that links atomic-scale charge redistribution, binding site geometry, and catalytic function is lacking.
decision.lever: Perform real-time X-ray absorption spectroscopy combined with operando vibrational spectroscopy under standard reaction conditions to map evolution of local electronic structure and adsorbate bonding on transition-metal catalysts with carefully controlled surface structure and composition. Vary the reaction environment (temperature, feed composition) while monitoring spectral shifts in metal d-band centers, oxidation states, and adsorbate signatures to establish correlations with measured activity, selectivity, and durability relative to a well-characterized baseline catalyst.
decision.why: Based on the trend in recent studies emphasizing local electronic effects and site-specific adsorption, in situ/operando electronic and vibrational probes offer a direct means to test whether shifts in orbital occupation and adsorbate binding energies truly govern catalytic performance. Tracking these factors in real time as reaction conditions evolve will clarify which mechanistic steps are most sensitive and thereby confirm or refute hypotheses about primary activity- or selectivity-determining features.
